I wish I had kept more of my communications on self driving, but they are on sites that no longer exist.

Not as long as 15 years ago, but over 5 years ago I came to the conclusion that self-driving would require general intelligence capable of conceptualizing. Driving has a lot of reacting, but it requires a lot of predicting to truly be effective. It also requires very low latency. Most of the reacting can be dealt with by deterministic processes, for example sensors that show a car has appeared in front of you.

The real issue with driving is future state prediction. A whole lot of driving safety is about completely avoiding bad positions in the first place. This is where you need a world model and an understanding of humans/animals/physics, etc.

We are really terrible at predicting what's easy and what's hard -- 15 years ago we were screaming at truck drivers to learn to code, lol. Another really fun story I like -- what if in the summer of 2020 (GPT-3 release) someone told you that language model was about as close to self-driving as Tesla's Autopilot was, with it's billions of miles of data and vision-first approach. Would have sounded nutty, but VLAs drive cars now. My lack of surprisal is mostly appreciating the uncertainty in dealing with unknowns.

But I generally agree, there's a lot of takes now about "RH fell, cancer is next", and I'm very skeptical. We'll probably see lots of progress in parts of biology or physics that already have ready-made verification systems, there's probably lots of business opportunities in building physical verifiers, and there's probably a lot potential in applying existing methods to larger data sets like the Vera Rubin telescope. But what if you need a 50B telescope and 20 years to build it in order to verify some physics hypothesis? What if you do need a RCT across a population to verify a new drug hypothesis? Progress will look a lot like classical progress then, despite AI.

I wouldn't go so far as to say that it's not surprising. I personally expected the slow march of progress to continue -- there's no reason why an IMO gold medal should be the peak -- but I never would have guessed that problems like RH or matrix multiplication would have been fully resolved this year. I don't think I'm alone, either: a month ago, Terry Tao said he expected some progress on RH by 2050!

That said, I do agree that there are similarities. My mental model of what's going on here is proof assistants have made math into a game-like environment, so much that we know about making superhuman game AI carries over to writing superhuman proofs. My biggest question now is whether other fields can be turned into games in the same way (is there a "drug discovery game"?). In that sense, I think the sim-to-real gap is alive and more important than ever.

Summary of the new results versus previous established bounds:

1. Integer factorization (randomized / Las Vegas):

- New: `L_N[1/3, 105]`

- Previous: L_N[1/2, 1]

In practice the General Number Field Sieve was assumed to run in L_N[1/3, 1.923] time. But it's unproven.

Here L_N[a,c] = exp((c+o(1)) * (log N)^a * (log log N)^(1-a)).

2. Discrete logarithms:

- New: exp((2+o(1)) * (log n)^2 / log log log n)

- Previous: exp(O((log n)^2))

So it wins by logloglogn in the denominator.

3. Approximate Nash equilibrium

- New: polynomial time for epsilon = 1/5

- Previous: polynomial time for epsilon = 1/3 + delta

4. Deterministic integer factorization

- New: exp(O((log N)^(3/4)))

- Previous established bound: N^(1/5+o(1))

5. Log-rank conjecture (How many bits do you need to communicate to compute a boolean function f(x,y) \in {0,1}?)

- New: O(r^0.499995)

- Previous: O(r^0.5)

6. Can you reconstruct a graph given all m subgraphs obtained by deleting exactly one edge?

- New: m >= 1000n

- Previous: m > n log_2(n)

I think the rest of your post is the argument! (Which I completely agree with.)

Factoring has just never been all that strong of a problem, especially not to trust encryption to.

Not following why factoring being easy would imply other quantum problems being harder. The entire field of quantum computing essentially sits on the stilts of Shor’s algorithm. It is the only clear end-to-end exponential algorithmic speedup. Because of this, people have conjectured that quantum computers would have exponential speedups for other problems too, but to date nothing else has reached the same clear utility as Shor’s. Other problems tend to fall into one of several categories:

1) modest polynomial speedups, like Grover’s algo, which also requires you prepare a quantum oracle. unclear if this ever beats a classical computer end to end for a practical problem

2) random circuit sampling (ie any claims of quantum “supremacy” to date), which solves no interesting problem

3) intrinsically quantum problems like Hamiltonian simulation for which it is unclear whether a QC actually has algorithmic advantage for interesting observables, as opposed to just being a good classical analog computer for solving such problems. These are exactly the problems that tend to fall to classical methods when sufficient compute and algorithmic advances are applied to them, and I suspect would fall especially quickly with AI assistance.

The fundamental problem is that once Shor was published, there has been a huge effort on the quantum side to figure out “what other problems can a QC solve?” but no incentive to press on the question of “but what if we applied a similar amount of effort on classical methods?” It doesn’t help that most of the problems studied in QC are somewhat niche and chosen specifically for how they play nice with QC, so there is little impetus to study them outside the community.

So, my thesis is this: if quantum’s one slam dunk advantage falls, all the other alleged advantages that came in its wake (but rest on much shakier ground) almost certainly fall too.

My prediction: factoring is in P, and Shor’s algorithm has been hinting that to us for decades. This magic algorithmic loophole that quantum physics seems to have found never sat right with me.

> If we solve factoring classicaly, there’s very little chance all those other problems don’t also have good-enough classical algorithms

Isn't it the exact opposite: if integer factoring is a weak problem, doesn't that mean other problems are likely to be harder?

Factoring has been known to be sketchy for decades; it's why people developed alternatives to RSA in the first place. If it falls into a non-galactic, practical classical algorithm, it would be big news but not break the universe of cryptography. So that doesn't say much about discrete logs.

Your broader point that quantum computers don't have much to offer here is entirely correct, though. Even the quantum factoring algorithms barely work.

Honestly, if factoring goes down the quantum industry is dead. It is the only useful algorithm with a known exponential speedup versus best known classical, everything else is just suggestive and involves a ton of hand waving. And like you said, any apparent quantum speedup tends to disappear for these other problems when enough attention and classical compute is brought in. If we solve factoring classicaly, there’s very little chance all those other problems don’t also have good-enough classical algorithms.

"Quantum Simulation", i.e. condensed matter, material science, really high-energy particle physics, and protein folding are the other "killer app" and are closer to reality than a quantum computer that can run "arithmetic" algorithms like Shor's. However AI (e.g. AlphaFold) has been providing disturbingly good advanced on that side too.

There are some other advantages to quantum technologies (sensing, some specific forms of secure communication, some forms of noise-resilience in networking) that are not to be discarded too.

> presumably they'll also cease their explosive R&D expenditures, so they'll be profitable if they can navigate the transition

They cannot cease these so easily, they are on the hook for almost a trillion in committed spending over the coming decade, this is what the market is pricing.

Even for investors who don't believe in recursive self-improvement, I think Anthropic's current valuation is unreasonably low.

They are currently valued at about US$1.1 trillion, and had US$17 billion of revenue last quarter, up from US$11.6 billion the quarter before, which amounts to doubling every 6 months (a slowdown; the previous quarter was up 145% from US$4.73 billion in revenue for Q1, which amounts to doubling every 4 months). They're committed to spending about US$70 billion over the next year. They're sitting on US$200 billion in cash, which is enough runway for about another year at their current burn rate, or two years if they had to strip bare because of big problems. The last debt they issued (US$60 billion) was at 10.5%, so they could probably borrow another year's worth if they needed to. That interest rate suggests that their creditors think they have about a 5% per year chance of going bankrupt. Their gross profit margin on the inference they sell is reportedly about 50%, so the only reason they're losing money now is that they're doing a lot of R&D.

This doesn't sound to me like the kind of situation where they are really at a major risk of bankruptcy in the next year. Indeed, it sounds to me like they're almost guaranteed to double their revenue in the next year, since currently they're doubling their revenue every 6 months, and their product is pretty sticky—once you've delegated your job or your company to Claude, you aren't getting it back. So any decline in their revenues would have to be pretty gradual.

If AI becomes "normal technology" and they cease their explosive growth, say a year from now, presumably they'll also cease their explosive R&D expenditures, so they'll be profitable if they can navigate the transition. I don't see how you could forecast their chances of bankruptcy in the process to be more than 50% (being able to borrow from Blackstone at 10.5% means that Blackstone estimates it as much lower) and so a risk-neutral investor would value them at something under 40 years of the profits they'd make if they come out the other side of that transition successfully, assuming their target P/E is 20 years.

Right now, those profits would be on the order of US$30 billion per year, which would justify US$1.2 trillion in valuation, which is higher than their current valuation. So investors who are selling today are either making a bet that, if Anthropic survives that traumatic transition, they'll have less revenues than they have now; or that their chances of bankruptcy in the next year or two are over 50%. Or they're just very, very risk-averse investors.
